title: Deluge Gun
primary_metric: effective gallons of water landing on target per minute (rated GPM discounted by each arc's modeled wind-drift loss)

options.A: The Low Arc — the flatter of the two solved elevation angles, favoring flow efficiency
options.B: The High Arc — the steeper complementary elevation angle, favoring obstruction clearance

sources.claim: Collapse zone standoff distance is set as a multiple of building height
sources.title: Establishing Collapse Zones At Building Fires (Christopher J. Naum)
sources.note: Quoted directly via fetch: 'This area is often defined by establishing a perimeter at a distance from the building that is equal to 1.5 times the height of the structure.' No formal code/standard is cited by the article for this specific multiplier, but it is widely repeated fire-service practice; used here as the case's real, hard-constraint rule.

sources.claim: Incident commanders should establish and visually mark a collapse zone during defensive structure-fire operations
sources.org: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH)
sources.title: Preventing Deaths & Injuries to Firefighters by Establishing Collapse Zones at Structure Fires, Workplace Solutions Publication No. 2014-120
sources.note: cdc.gov returned HTTP 403 to this case's automated fetch tool on every attempt, so the document's exact wording could not be directly quoted -- only its existence, title, and topic are confirmed (cross-referenced via multiple independent secondary sources, including S1). Used only as general supporting context for 'collapse zones are a real, recommended practice'; the specific 1.5× figure the case's math actually uses is cited to S1, not S2.

sources.claim: Smoothbore discharge formula (the Freeman Formula) and the standard operating pressure for smoothbore master-stream nozzles
sources.value: GPM = 29.71 d^2 sqrt(NP); standard NP = 80 psi
sources.title: Deck Guns: Know Your Flow (Joseph R. Polenzani)
sources.note: Quoted directly via fetch. Article notes other published coefficients exist (29.83 AIA, 29.84 NFPA, 29.7 IFSTA/Jones & Bartlett) -- all close to 29.71, none of which changes this case's conclusions materially.

sources.claim: Published rated discharge for a 1-3/8 in smoothbore master-stream tip at 80 psi
sources.title: Fixed Master Stream Operations Using Smooth Bore Tips (Paul Shapiro)
sources.note: Quoted directly via fetch from the article's stacked-tip table: '1 3/8-inch  502 gpm'. Used to cross-check the monitor's own 500 GPM rating (S6) -- the two independent real sources agree within 0.4%.

sources.claim: Idealized (no-drag) projectile range formula and the fact that two complementary launch angles produce the identical range
sources.value: R = v0^2 sin(2*theta0) / g; example pair 15 deg / 75 deg both give R = 128 m at v0 = 50 m/s
sources.title: University Physics Volume 1, Section 4.3 'Motion in Two and Three Dimensions' — Projectile Motion, Equation 4.26
sources.note: Quoted directly via fetch, including the text: 'It is interesting that the same range is found for two initial launch angles that sum to 90 degrees.' g = 32.2 ft/s^2 is the standard US-customary equivalent of the same physical constant used in this formula and does not itself require a separate citation.

sources.claim: Elevation range and maximum rated flow of a real, currently-sold high-elevation portable fire monitor
sources.value: 10 deg to 86 deg elevation; 500 GPM max flow
sources.title: BlitzFire High Elevation Oscillating Portable Monitor, model XX232A-HE, product page
sources.note: Quoted directly via fetch. Standard (non-HE) BlitzFire models cap at 46 deg elevation; the HE variant used here is the one whose real elevation range (10-86 deg) contains both this case's solved angles (~19.2 deg and ~70.8 deg).

deliverables.text: A velocity-component verification worksheet: for each arc, compute the horizontal and vertical velocity components from the solved angle and the nozzle's derived exit velocity, then use the Pythagorean identity to verify, showing algebra, that the components recombine to the nozzle's rated exit velocity.

A two-angle solution worksheet: solve the range equation's resulting trigonometric equation for the elevation angle over the interval 0 to 90 degrees, showing both valid solutions (Low Arc and High Arc) with the inverse trig evaluation shown step by step.

A hang-time and clearance comparison: compute time of flight and apex height for each arc, then compute each arc's actual height at the parapet remnant's horizontal distance and state whether it clears the remnant.
An effective-flow table: apply the wind-drift loss model to each arc's rated flow to find effective gallons-on-target per minute, and state the margin between the two arcs.
An original visual (Challenge 2b): a labeled diagram or graph of both trajectories, with each arc's elevation angle marked in both degrees and radians, and apex heights labeled.

appendices.title: The Real Doctrine and the Real Formula
How To… Math Questions To Research

balance.argument_a: At theta = 19.21 degrees, the Low Arc spends only 2.21 seconds airborne versus the High Arc's 6.33 seconds -- under the case's 2% per second wind-drift loss rate, that is 477.93 effective GPM landing on target for the Low Arc versus 436.65 for the High Arc, a 9.45% edge over the High Arc. Less time in the air is less time for wind to steal flow off the target, full stop.
balance.argument_b: The High Arc's 70.79 degree elevation sends it to a 161.5 ft apex versus the Low Arc's 19.6 ft -- roughly 8x higher -- which is why it drops down almost vertically instead of skimming the 225 ft stand-off at head height the whole way through the collapse zone's own debris field. A 9.45% flow edge is worth nothing if the Low Arc's low, flat 19.6 ft path is the one more likely to be deflected by debris before it ever reaches the target 225 ft away.
balance.margin_basis: Compare effective gallons-on-target per minute for the Low Arc vs. the High Arc: rated GPM (Appendix B) discounted by the wind-drift loss model (Appendix F, MA2) applied to each arc's own time of flight (computed in D3).

modeling_assumptions.statement: The fictional structure's height, used with the real 1.5x collapse-zone rule (S1) to set the mandated stand-off distance R.
modeling_assumptions.why: No real address exists to cite -- Ridgeview Fire Department and this incident are a scenario construction. 150 ft is an ordinary height for the kind of mixed-use commercial structure that gets a defensive, collapse-zone response; the multiplier rule applied to that height (1.5x) is real and cited (S1).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Both solved elevation angles (Appendix C / D2) depend directly on R -- a different assumed height changes both solved angles. A Hero who assumes a different height should expect different angle solutions, though still a complementary pair within the monitor's real 10-86 degree elevation range (S6).

modeling_assumptions.statement: The wind-drift loss rate applied to each arc's rated flow, per second of time of flight: 2% of rated flow lost per second of flight.
modeling_assumptions.why: Real fire-service doctrine holds, qualitatively, that a stream spends more time exposed to crosswind the longer it is airborne, and that this reduces how much of its rated flow actually lands on target -- but no public source publishes a specific numeric loss-rate-per-second for a master stream. This case states one illustrative rate rather than presenting an invented number as if it were measured.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the case's single most load-bearing assumption -- the answer to D4's margin is sensitive to this value. A Hero who argues for a different rate, and shows how it changes the effective-flow comparison, is doing exactly the T4 work this case is built to require.

modeling_assumptions.statement: The collapsed parapet remnant's height (12 ft) and its horizontal distance from the monitor (a fixed 200 ft, independent of MA1).
modeling_assumptions.why: No real address or remnant exists to cite -- like the structure height (MA1), this is a stated scenario figure. 12 ft is a plausible height for a partial parapet collapse. The 200 ft distance is stated as a FIXED physical fact of this specific incident, deliberately independent of MA1 -- a hypothetical taller or shorter structure (the kind of what-if Socratic Question 4 invites) does not relocate a real, already-collapsed piece of debris; it only changes the mandated stand-off distance R new water has to travel to reach the target beyond it.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: D3 asks students to compute each arc's actual height at this distance (using the trajectory-height formula in Appendix C), not just the apex -- this was added specifically so the case's clearance claim is checkable against a real number rather than asserted from the apex heights alone. CONFIRMED during Tier 2 P4 adjudication (2026-08-20, verified independently by two fresh subagents): even holding MA3's 200 ft parapet distance fixed (the stated, non-scaling convention), the Low Arc's clearance verdict is genuinely fragile to MA1 alone -- it crosses from blocked (7.77 ft at the stated 150 ft) to clearing at approximately MA1 = 159 ft, only ~6% above the case's stated value. This is materially more fragile than the primary metric (D4's 9.45% margin, which is robust across MA1's full +/-50% flex per sensitivity_model.py / Tier 2 P5). This fragility is disclosed, not hidden: FACILITATOR.md's Question 4 note states the exact crossover point and frames it as a legitimate discussion finding rather than a defect to dodge.

sensitivity_note: LOW-MODERATE (SPEC §6). This case is set at an active structure fire with a declared collapse zone, which carries real weight, but the math never asks a student to reason about casualties or injury -- every deliverable is about water delivery and stream geometry (protection framing). Facilitators should give a one-line flag before Launch, since 'structure fire, collapse risk' can land heavily for a Hero with a personal connection to fire service.
